Claude Certified Architect – Foundations · CCAR-F

Nail the exam at one hundred percent — by answering the right questions in any scenario.

Sixty items. One hundred twenty minutes. One durable setup — not prompt tricks. Official-doc provenance. High-yield drills. No hype. Not a leaked item bank — public guide objectives only.

Verified against official Anthropic docs 2026-08-01. Progress is local to this browser session.

D1 27%D2 18%D3 20%D4 20%D5 15%

D1 · 27% of exam

Agentic Architecture & Orchestration

Marcus builds a support agent that keeps talking after it should have finished. He added a max-iteration cap and started parsing the assistant text for done. That is the stall — and it is not a model problem. It is a stop_reason setup problem, and it is fixable.

The one move: While stop_reason is tool_use, run the tool and send the result back. When it's end_turn, stop. Subagents get a clean room — you pass what they need.

Procedure

  1. Send request (tools + messages)
  2. Inspect stop_reason
  3. If tool_use → execute tools
  4. Append tool_result (matched ids)
  5. Repeat until non-tool_use

Teach

The agentic loop (one move)

Send a request with tools. If stop_reason is tool_use, execute those tools, append tool_result blocks (and only those) to history, call again. If stop_reason is end_turn (or max_tokens, refusal, etc.), stop the tool loop. Do not parse natural language for done.

Hub-and-spoke multi-agent

The coordinator holds the plan. Subagents run in isolated context — they do not inherit the parent's chat. Pass findings explicitly in the spawn prompt. Route communication through the coordinator for observability.

Agent tool (formerly Task)

Spawning uses the Agent tool (Task remains an alias in some SDK surfaces). allowed tools must include Agent/Task. Parallel spawn = multiple Agent calls in one response.

Hooks beat prompts for hard rules

Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate when money or identity is on the line. PreToolUse can block a refund above threshold. PostToolUse can normalize timestamps before the model sees them. Soft guidance stays in CLAUDE.md; hard guarantees use hooks.

Anti-patterns

SkipUse
Parse assistant text for loop terminationBranch on stop_reason only
Arbitrary iteration caps as primary stopstop_reason end_turn / non-tool_use exits
Assume subagents share parent memoryPass complete findings in the spawn prompt
Reliability only in system promptHooks / prerequisite gates for deterministic rules

Task statements

TS 1.1 Design and implement agentic loops for autonomous task execution

Knowledge: The agentic loop lifecycle: sending requests to Claude, inspecting stop_reason ("tool_use" vs "end_turn"), executing requested tools, and returning results for the next iteration; How tool results are appended to conversation history so the model can reason about the next action

TS 1.2 Orchestrate multi-agent systems with coordinator-subagent patterns

Knowledge: Hub-and-spoke architecture where a coordinator agent manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and information routing; How subagents operate with isolated context—they do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history automatically

TS 1.3 Configure subagent invocation, context passing, and spawning

Knowledge: The Task tool as the mechanism for spawning subagents, and the requirement that allowedTools must include "Task" for a coordinator to invoke subagents; That subagent context must be explicitly provided in the prompt—subagents do not automatically inherit parent context or share memory between invocations

TS 1.4 Implement multi-step workflows with enforcement and handoff patterns

Knowledge: The difference between programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) and prompt-based guidance for workflow ordering; When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial operations), prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate

TS 1.5 Apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization

Knowledge: Hook patterns (e.g., PostToolUse) that intercept tool results for transformation before the model processes them; Hook patterns that intercept outgoing tool calls to enforce compliance rules (e.g., blocking refunds above a threshold)

TS 1.6 Design task decomposition strategies for complex workflows

Knowledge: When to use fixed sequential pipelines (prompt chaining) versus dynamic adaptive decomposition based on intermediate findings; Prompt chaining patterns that break reviews into sequential steps (e.g., analyze each file individually, then run a cross-file integration pass)

TS 1.7 Manage session state, resumption, and forking

Knowledge: Named session resumption using --resume <session-name> to continue a specific prior conversation; fork_session for creating independent branches from a shared analysis baseline to explore divergent approaches

Drill

Q1

In any agentic loop, what are the steps of a single iteration from sending a request to sending the next one, and which single field decides whether the loop continues?

lists send request -> read stop_reason -> if tool_use execute tools -> append results -> resend · identifies stop_reason as the sole continuation signal · names the request-shaping fields the loop sets per request: max_tokens and the system prompt

Q2

A teammate proposes ending the loop when the assistant's text contains 'TASK COMPLETE' - what makes this an anti-pattern, and what should signal completion instead?

natural-language signals are probabilistic and phrasing-dependent - the model may omit or emit them spuriously · stop_reason end_turn is the structured, reliable completion signal

Q3

Why can a subagent not simply 'know' what the coordinator or a sibling learned earlier, and what does that force the coordinator to do?

subagents run with isolated context - no automatic inheritance of coordinator history or sibling results · coordinator must explicitly route needed information into each subagent's prompt · forgetting this yields subagents that redo work or answer generically

Q4

Every subagent in a research pipeline succeeded, yet the final report covers only a narrow slice of the topic - where do you look first for the root cause and why?

look at the coordinator's task decomposition - the subtasks it assigned define maximum possible coverage · subagents executing narrow assignments correctly cannot recover breadth that was never assigned · blaming search queries, analysis filters, or synthesis instructions misreads correct downstream behavior

Q5

A coordinator's Task tool calls silently never spawn anything - what configuration must you check first, and what is the general rule it instantiates?

check that 'Task' is included in the coordinator's allowedTools · rule: subagent spawning is itself a tool call and is gated by tool permissions like any other

D2 · 18% of exam

Tool Design & MCP Integration

Maya has eighteen tools and the agent keeps calling the wrong one. She rewrote the system prompt three times. The fix is smaller: four tools with sharp descriptions, not eighteen with one-liners.

The one move: Tool descriptions are how Claude picks the tool. Write them like a careful colleague brief. MCP is USB-C for tools: tools the model calls, resources the app feeds, prompts the user invokes.

Procedure

  1. Design clear tool boundaries
  2. Write rich descriptions
  3. Set tool_choice for the turn
  4. Handle tool_result / is_error
  5. Wire MCP servers by scope

Teach

Descriptions over clever schemas

Say what the tool does, when to use it, when not to, inputs, outputs, and edge cases — three to four sentences minimum. Rename overlapping tools. Split generic analyze_document into purpose-specific tools.

tool_choice modes

auto: model may answer in text. any: must call some tool. forced name: must call that tool first. none: no tools. Forced any/tool prefills so there is no natural language before the call.

Structured errors

Return is_error with category (transient / validation / permission / business), isRetryable, and a clear description. Generic Operation failed wastes retries.

MCP scopes and .mcp.json

Project .mcp.json is shared team tooling with env expansion. User ~/.claude.json is personal. Prefer HTTP for remote servers; stdio for local. Resources expose catalogs so agents stop exploratory fishing.

Anti-patterns

SkipUse
18 overlapping tools on one agent4–5 role-scoped tools
Uniform Operation failedStructured is_error + retry flags
Secrets committed in .mcp.json${GITHUB_TOKEN} expansion
Treat resources as model-invoked toolsResources are application-driven context

Task statements

TS 2.1 Design effective tool interfaces with clear descriptions and boundaries

Knowledge: Tool descriptions as the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection; minimal descriptions lead to unreliable selection among similar tools; The importance of including input formats, example queries, edge cases, and boundary explanations in tool descriptions

TS 2.2 Implement structured error responses for MCP tools

Knowledge: The MCP isError flag pattern for communicating tool failures back to the agent; The distinction between transient errors (timeouts, service unavailability), validation errors (invalid input), business errors (policy violations), and permission errors

TS 2.3 Distribute tools appropriately across agents and configure tool choice

Knowledge: The principle that giving an agent access to too many tools (e.g., 18 instead of 4-5) degrades tool selection reliability by increasing decision complexity; Why agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them (e.g., a synthesis agent attempting web searches)

TS 2.4 Integrate MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows

Knowledge: MCP server scoping: project-level (.mcp.json) for shared team tooling vs user-level (~/.claude.json) for personal/experimental servers; Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json (e.g., ${GITHUB_TOKEN}) for credential management without committing secrets

TS 2.5 Select and apply built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) effectively

Knowledge: Grep for content search (searching file contents for patterns like function names, error messages, or import statements); Glob for file path pattern matching (finding files by name or extension patterns)

Drill

Q1

Users ask about orders and the agent calls get_customer instead of lookup_order; both have one-line descriptions - what is the most effective first step and why is it first?

expand each description: input formats handled, example queries, edge cases, boundaries versus the similar tool · descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for selection - minimal ones are the root cause · first because low-effort/high-leverage: few-shot adds tokens without fixing the cause; routing layers and tool consolidation are heavier redesigns

Q2

analyze_content and analyze_document have near-identical descriptions and get misrouted constantly - what rename-and-describe move fixes it, and what makes a name self-disambiguating?

rename to reflect the actual domain, e.g. analyze_content -> extract_web_results with a web-specific description · self-disambiguating: the name itself encodes the input domain or action so overlap disappears at a glance · name and description must agree - a good name with a generic description still misroutes

Q3

What does a well-structured MCP tool error response contain, and what does the isError flag itself communicate?

isError flag marks the result as a failure the agent must reason about (MCP's failure-communication pattern) · errorCategory (transient/validation/permission), isRetryable boolean, human-readable description · each field maps to a distinct agent decision: what happened, whether to retry, what to say

Q4

A search returns nothing - how must the tool distinguish 'no matches exist' from 'could not access the source', and what wrong behavior follows from conflating them?

valid empty result = successful query with zero matches; access failure = error needing a retry decision · conflation as failure triggers pointless retries of a correct answer · conflation as success silently drops recoverable data from the research

Q5

A synthesis agent needs frequent simple fact-checks but full search access violates its role; round-tripping through the coordinator adds 40% latency - what design resolves this, and why not the extremes?

give it a scoped verify_fact tool for the high-frequency simple case · complex verifications still delegate through the coordinator to the search agent · full search access over-provisions and violates separation of concerns; batching creates blocking dependencies; speculative caching cannot predict needs

D3 · 20% of exam

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows

Sam joins the repo and none of the coding standards fire. They lived in the previous developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. That is not a people problem. It is a hierarchy problem.

The one move: CLAUDE.md is the room that remembers. Put team standards in the project file, personal habits in the user file, and path-specific rules in .claude/rules/ so they only load when needed.

Procedure

  1. Place standards at correct hierarchy level
  2. Split topic rules into .claude/rules/
  3. Add path globs where needed
  4. Create skills for on-demand workflows
  5. Choose plan mode vs direct by complexity

Teach

CLAUDE.md hierarchy

User (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) is personal and not shared. Project (.claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md) is team and versioned. Directory-level files scope further. Use @import and .claude/rules/ for modular rules.

Path-specific rules

YAML frontmatter paths globs load rules only when matching files are edited — better token economy than dumping everything into one CLAUDE.md. Prefer globs for **/*.test.tsx over directory-only files when tests are spread out.

Skills vs always-on memory

Skills in .claude/skills/ are on-demand workflows with frontmatter (context: fork, allowed-tools, argument-hint). CLAUDE.md is always-loaded standards. Use context: fork so verbose analysis does not pollute the main session.

Plan mode vs direct execution

Plan mode for multi-file architectural decisions. Direct execution for a single well-scoped change. Do not plan a one-line validation fix.

Anti-patterns

SkipUse
Team standards only in user CLAUDE.mdProject-level CLAUDE.md in git
Monolithic 2k-line CLAUDE.md.claude/rules/ + @import
Verbose skill in main contextcontext: fork isolation
Plan mode for one-line editsDirect execution for small scope

Task statements

TS 3.1 Configure CLAUDE.md files with appropriate hierarchy, scoping, and modular organization

Knowledge: The CLAUDE.md configuration hierarchy: user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project-level (.claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md), and directory-level (subdirectory CLAUDE.md files); That user-level settings apply only to that user—instructions in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md are not shared with teammates via version control

TS 3.2 Create and configure custom slash commands and skills

Knowledge: Project-scoped commands in .claude/commands/ (shared via version control) vs user-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/ (personal); Skills in .claude/skills/ with SKILL.md files that support frontmatter configuration including context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint

TS 3.3 Apply path-specific rules for conditional convention loading

Knowledge: .claude/rules/ files with YAML frontmatter paths fields containing glob patterns for conditional rule activation; How path-scoped rules load only when editing matching files, reducing irrelevant context and token usage

TS 3.4 Determine when to use plan mode vs direct execution

Knowledge: Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, architectural decisions, and multi-file modifications; Direct execution is appropriate for simple, well-scoped changes (e.g., adding a single validation check to one function)

TS 3.5 Apply iterative refinement techniques for progressive improvement

Knowledge: Concrete input/output examples as the most effective way to communicate expected transformations when prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently; Test-driven iteration: writing test suites first, then iterating by sharing test failures to guide progressive improvement

TS 3.6 Integrate Claude Code into CI/CD pipelines

Knowledge: The -p (or --print) flag for running Claude Code in non-interactive mode in automated pipelines; --output-format json and --json-schema CLI flags for enforcing structured output in CI contexts

Drill

Q1

A new team member's Claude Code ignores conventions everyone else gets - what misplacement explains it and what is the fix?

the conventions live in someone's user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which is not shared via version control · fix: move team-wide instructions to project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repo · general law: sharing scope is determined by which level holds the instruction

Q2

Your CLAUDE.md mixes testing, API, and deployment guidance and has become unmanageable - what reorganization does Claude Code support and what does each resulting file look like?

split into focused topic files in .claude/rules/ (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md) · each file carries one coherent concern, independently maintainable · this replaces the monolithic CLAUDE.md pattern for large rule sets

Q3

A /review command must be available to every developer the moment they clone or pull the repo - where does the file go, and why do the plausible alternatives fail?

create it in .claude/commands/ inside the repository - version control distributes it · ~/.claude/commands/ is personal and unshared; CLAUDE.md holds instructions, not command definitions · no commands array in a config JSON exists

Q4

A codebase-analysis skill floods the main conversation with exploratory output - which frontmatter option fixes it, and what exactly changes at runtime?

context: fork - the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context · verbose/exploratory output stays in the fork; only results return to the main session · same option applies to brainstorming skills whose exploration should not persist

Q5

Write the skeleton of a path-scoped rule file for Terraform conventions - what frontmatter field and value make it conditional?

a .claude/rules/ file with YAML frontmatter containing paths: ["terraform/**/*"] · the body holds the conventions; the paths globs are the activation condition

D4 · 20% of exam

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output

Linda's review bot flooded the team with style nits. Devs muted every category — including the security ones that worked. Trust is global. Noise in one place taxes everything.

The one move: Vague be conservative does not cut false positives. Explicit categories do. tool_use with a schema kills bad JSON. Independent review beats self-review because the generator keeps its own justifications.

Procedure

  1. Write decidable criteria + severity examples
  2. Add 2–4 few-shot on ambiguous cases
  3. Force schema via tool_use + tool_choice
  4. Validate + retry with error feedback
  5. Review in independent multi-pass architecture

Teach

Explicit criteria, not confidence dials

Report bugs and security issues; skip style and local patterns. Attach severity examples. Temporarily disable noisy categories until precision recovers.

Few-shot when instructions still drift

Two to four targeted examples on ambiguous cases. Show the reasoning, not only the input-output pair. Include format examples and varied document structures for extraction.

Structured output via tool_use

JSON schema via tool_use eliminates syntax errors. It does not fix semantic errors (sums that do not add up). Nullable fields prevent fabrication of missing data. Enums need unclear and other escape hatches.

Batch API and review architecture

Batch is 50 percent cheaper, up to about 24 hours, no latency SLA, no multi-turn tool loops. Keep pre-merge checks synchronous. Review in independent instances; large PRs get per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass.

Anti-patterns

SkipUse
be conservative / high-confidence onlyCategorical report vs skip criteria
Required fields for optional source dataNullable + prompt-side normalization
Batch for blocking pre-merge checksBatch only latency-tolerant work
Generator reviews its own output in-sessionIndependent review instance

Task statements

TS 4.1 Design prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives

Knowledge: The importance of explicit criteria over vague instructions (e.g., "flag comments only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior" vs "check that comments are accurate"); How general instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" fail to improve precision compared to specific categorical criteria

TS 4.2 Apply few-shot prompting to improve output consistency and quality

Knowledge: Few-shot examples as the most effective technique for achieving consistently formatted, actionable output when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results; The role of few-shot examples in demonstrating ambiguous-case handling (e.g., tool selection for ambiguous requests, branch-level test coverage gaps)

TS 4.3 Enforce structured output using tool use and JSON schemas

Knowledge: Tool use (tool_use) with JSON schemas as the most reliable approach for guaranteed schema-compliant structured output, eliminating JSON syntax errors; The distinction between tool_choice: "auto" (model may return text instead of calling a tool), "any" (model must call a tool but can choose which), and forced tool selection (model must call a specific named tool)

TS 4.4 Implement validation, retry, and feedback loops for extraction quality

Knowledge: Retry-with-error-feedback: appending specific validation errors to the prompt on retry to guide the model toward correction; The limits of retry: retries are ineffective when the required information is simply absent from the source document (vs format or structural errors)

TS 4.5 Design efficient batch processing strategies

Knowledge: The Message Batches API: 50% cost savings, up to 24-hour processing window, no guaranteed latency SLA; Batch processing is appropriate for non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads (overnight reports, weekly audits, nightly test generation) and inappropriate for blocking workflows (pre-merge checks)

TS 4.6 Design multi-instance and multi-pass review architectures

Knowledge: Self-review limitations: a model retains reasoning context from generation, making it less likely to question its own decisions in the same session; Independent review instances (without prior reasoning context) are more effective at catching subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking

Drill

Q1

You added 'be conservative and only report high-confidence findings' and the false positive rate did not move - why do such instructions fail, and what class of instruction works?

confidence-based filtering gives the model no operational definition of what to skip · specific categorical criteria work: report bugs and security issues, skip minor style and local patterns · the model needs category boundaries, not a dial for a confidence it cannot calibrate

Q2

One review category produces mostly noise and developers have started dismissing everything - what is the immediate move and what is its exit condition?

temporarily disable the high false-positive categories · keep accurate categories running so trust can rebuild on real signal · re-enable a category once its improved prompt demonstrates acceptable precision

Q3

Detailed instructions still yield inconsistently formatted, hit-or-miss output - what technique do you reach for, with how many examples, targeted at what?

add few-shot examples - the most effective technique for consistent, actionable output · 2-4 targeted examples, not a large pile · target the ambiguous scenarios where behavior actually diverges

Q4

Extraction returns empty/null for required fields that ARE present in oddly formatted documents - what is the few-shot fix and why does it also reduce hallucination?

add examples showing correct extraction from documents with varied formats (informal measurements, unusual layouts) · the model learns to recognize the information despite surface variation · demonstrated grounded extraction reduces both misses and fabricated values

Q5

What precisely may and must the model do under tool_choice auto, any, and forced - and in which one situation is each the right setting?

auto: may call a tool or answer in text - right for genuinely optional tool use · any: must call some tool, model picks which - right when structure is mandatory but the schema choice is the model's · forced {type:'tool',name:...}: must call that tool - right when one specific extraction must run

D5 · 15% of exam

Context Management & Reliability

A forty-turn refund chat misquotes the amount after progressive summarization. The agent is not being careless. The facts fell out of the summary. Put them on a shelf the summary cannot throw away.

The one move: Exact numbers die in vague summaries. Keep transactional facts in a case-facts block. Escalate on explicit request, policy gaps, and no progress — not on sentiment.

Procedure

  1. Extract case-facts each turn
  2. Trim tool results at ingestion
  3. Escalate by explicit policy only
  4. Propagate structured errors with partials
  5. Preserve claim-source maps in synthesis

Teach

Preserve critical facts

Extract amounts, dates, order IDs, statuses into a persistent case-facts block outside summarized history. Still pass full history for coherence. Trim tool outputs at ingestion — not after the window is already full.

Lost-in-the-middle

Lead with key findings. Use section headers. Require metadata on subagent outputs so synthesis stays accurate.

Escalation policy

Legitimate triggers: customer asks for a human, policy exception/gap, inability to progress. Explicit demand escalates immediately. Frustration on a solvable issue: acknowledge and offer to resolve; escalate if they reiterate. Multiple identity matches → ask for more identifiers, never pick heuristically.

Error propagation and provenance

Propagate failure type, attempted query, partials, alternatives. No silent empty-as-success. Keep claim-source mappings through synthesis. Annotate conflicts; do not pick one number arbitrarily.

Anti-patterns

SkipUse
Summarize away exact amountsPersistent case-facts block
Escalate on sentiment / self-confidenceExplicit, policy-gap, no-progress triggers
Heuristic pick among three customer matchesAsk for more identifiers
Empty results marked successfulStructured error + partials upward

Task statements

TS 5.1 Manage conversation context to preserve critical information across long interactions

Knowledge: Progressive summarization risks: condensing numerical values, percentages, dates, and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries; The "lost in the middle" effect: models reliably process information at the beginning and end of long inputs but may omit findings from middle sections

TS 5.2 Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns

Knowledge: Appropriate escalation triggers: customer requests for a human, policy exceptions/gaps (not just complex cases), and inability to make meaningful progress; The distinction between escalating immediately when a customer explicitly demands it versus offering to resolve when the issue is straightforward

TS 5.3 Implement error propagation strategies across multi-agent systems

Knowledge: Structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternative approaches) as enabling intelligent coordinator recovery decisions; The distinction between access failures (timeouts needing retry decisions) and valid empty results (successful queries with no matches)

TS 5.4 Manage context effectively in large codebase exploration

Knowledge: Context degradation in extended sessions: models start giving inconsistent answers and referencing "typical patterns" rather than specific classes discovered earlier; The role of scratchpad files for persisting key findings across context boundaries

TS 5.5 Design human review workflows and confidence calibration

Knowledge: The risk that aggregate accuracy metrics (e.g., 97% overall) may mask poor performance on specific document types or fields; Stratified random sampling for measuring error rates in high-confidence extractions and detecting novel error patterns

TS 5.6 Preserve information provenance and handle uncertainty in multi-source synthesis

Knowledge: How source attribution is lost during summarization steps when findings are compressed without preserving claim-source mappings; The importance of structured claim-source mappings that the synthesis agent must preserve and merge when combining findings

Drill

Q1

After progressive summarization, the agent misquotes the refund amount and promised dates - what got lost, and what structure prevents it?

summaries condensed exact numbers, dates, and customer-stated expectations into vague prose · extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses) into a persistent case-facts block · the block rides in every prompt outside the summarized history, immune to compression

Q2

Findings from the middle of a long aggregated input keep getting omitted - what is the effect called, what are the two structural mitigations, and what must subagent outputs carry for synthesis to stay accurate?

the lost-in-the-middle effect: beginning and end process reliably, middles get dropped · mitigate: key-findings summary at the beginning, detailed results organized with explicit section headers · subagent outputs must include metadata (dates, source locations, methodological context) so downstream synthesis stays accurate

Q3

First-contact resolution is far below target: the agent escalates straightforward damage claims yet attempts policy-exception cases alone - what fix addresses the root cause, and why do confidence thresholds, trained classifiers, and sentiment routing all miss it?

root cause: unclear decision boundaries - add explicit escalation criteria with few-shot escalate-vs-resolve examples to the system prompt · self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated (the agent is already wrongly confident); classifiers are over-engineering before prompt optimization is tried · sentiment tracks emotion, not case complexity - a different variable entirely

Q4

get_customer returns three plausible matches - what must the agent do, and why is picking the best-looking match an anti-pattern?

ask the customer for additional identifiers to disambiguate · heuristic selection risks acting on the wrong account - misdirected refunds and privacy exposure · clarification is the required response to identity ambiguity

Q5

A web-search subagent times out mid-research - what exactly should it return to the coordinator, and what recovery option does each element unlock?

failure type (what happened) -> retry-vs-abandon; attempted query -> retry with modification · partial results -> proceed with what exists; potential alternatives -> redirect strategy · the payload is designed backward from the coordinator's decision space
